claims.text: The initial HEA is a single-phase solid solution.
The initial HEA has a homogeneous microstructure.
The initial HEA has high ductility and toughness.
Mechanical loading at high strain rates and service-relevant temperatures activates local compositional segregation and nanoscale precipitation.
Nanoscale precipitates inhibit dislocation motion and reduce the effective slip distance.
The loading-induced microstructural evolution causes a loss of toughness and a transition toward brittle fracture.
Stress concentrations promote the formation of nanoscale precipitates or local phase segregation.
Local energy fluctuations under high mechanical load destabilize the uniform solid solution and nucleate nanoscale precipitates.
Precipitates acting as slip obstacles reduce ductility and toughness and facilitate brittle fracture.
Critical combinations of strain rate and temperature will produce an observable onset of nanoscale precipitation or compositional segregation.
The onset of precipitation or segregation will be accompanied by a measurable decrease in toughness.
Fracture morphology will change from ductile dimpling to brittle cleavage.
The loading-induced microstructural evolution will change strain-hardening behavior.
The baseline as-cast alloy has a uniform, single-phase microstructure and fails ductilely with high toughness under comparable tests.
The proposed effect occurs when service loading generates sufficient localized stress but not when temperature is high enough to re-homogenize the alloy.
Conditions outside the stated strain-rate and temperature boundaries may not trigger phase evolution.
Strain rates from approximately 10^-3 to 10^2–10^3 s^-1 and temperatures from room temperature to 1073 K represent the applicable harsh-service regime.
